# 89:1/q03 What does al-fajr designate in the oath? [ٱلْفَجْرِ · referent]
turns on: Whether the noun denotes daily dawn, a whole day or prayer, a particular date or place, or a bursting spring or other emergence.
- 89:1/q03/p1 The familiar dawn occurring every day, taken generally.
  reasons: Ibn Abbas locates it in the east; al-Qurazi extends it daily until the world's end. Razi's Ibn Abbas report includes true and false dawn and says light ends night, sends creatures to provision and pictures resurrection (74:34; 81:18; 6:96). Alusi especially favors true dawn for its prayer and fasting role. Abu Hayyan, Ibn Ashur and Tabatabai prefer generic dawn; Ibn Ashur cites its coordination with night. Elmalili calls it the joyful move into light (81:18). Bint al-Shati uses 2:187 against extending it to the whole day; Muhammad Abduh likewise treats dawn and the ten nights generically. Baydawi compares 81:18 and Nasafi 74:34. Al-Suyuti identifies the oath's dawn as the beginning of the day.

  reasons: Mujahid excludes every ordinary dawn. Abu Muslim links it to offerings and the ten nights' culmination. Razi recalls Abrahamic rites and 37:107. Study Quran cites 2:196-197 and 22:27-29.

# 74:34/q03 What does 'asfara' mean here? [أَسْفَرَ · meaning]
- 74:34/q03/p1 Dawn becomes bright, clear, and visible as darkness gives way.
  reasons: Ibn Qutayba, al-Tabari, Qatada, al-Qushayri, al-Wahidi, al-Wahidi's Wajiz, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Bursevi and al-Alusi gloss it as brightening or becoming clear; al-Tabari and Qatada add that morning comes on. Ibn Atiyya says its light spreads before sunrise. Al-Tabrisi says it clears darkness and reveals visible things. Jishumi calls isfar appearance and visibility, citing sufur for a woman appearing without her veil; his account of safara says both forms can mean brightening, perhaps like a woman uncovering her face. Al-Wahidi and al-Razi cite the prophetic dawn-prayer wording, and both compare the radiant faces of 80:38; al-Wahidi says prayer waits until light is evident and doubt is removed. Al-Qurtubi says the light brightens and adds the images of a shining face, an unveiled woman's face, and a broom sweeping darkness from a house. Al-Raghib, reported by Bursevi, distinguishes safara for removing a physical covering from asfara for a color becoming clear and bright; Bursevi says isfar can mean entering dawn time. Al-Samin calls the removal of darkness from dawn's face a metaphor. Ibn al-Sumayfi and Isa ibn al-Fadl's safara is explained by Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi as stripping darkness from dawn's face. Qut al-qulub, reported by Bursevi, describes the second dawn as the sun's white glow beneath red twilight before the solar disk appears: sunset goes red, white, dark, and sunrise reverses the sequence. Al-Tabatabai calls isfar dawn's clearing and unveiling. Al-Damghani glosses asfara as dawn brightening and becoming clear. Al-Suyuti's Itqan reports a proposed etymology of tafsir from reversed safar, illustrated by dawn brightening; he also reports derivations from fasr and a physician's diagnostic test.

# 74:34/q03 What does 'asfara' mean here? [أَسْفَرَ · meaning]
- 74:34/q03/p1 Dawn becomes bright, clear, and visible as darkness gives way.
  reasons: Ibn Qutayba, al-Tabari, Qatada, al-Qushayri, al-Wahidi, al-Wahidi's Wajiz, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Bursevi and al-Alusi gloss it as brightening or becoming clear; al-Tabari and Qatada add that morning comes on. Ibn Atiyya says its light spreads before sunrise. Al-Tabrisi says it clears darkness and reveals visible things. Jishumi calls isfar appearance and visibility, citing sufur for a woman appearing without her veil; his account of safara says both forms can mean brightening, perhaps like a woman uncovering her face. Al-Wahidi and al-Razi cite the prophetic dawn-prayer wording, and both compare the radiant faces of 80:38; al-Wahidi says prayer waits until light is evident and doubt is removed. Al-Qurtubi says the light brightens and adds the images of a shining face, an unveiled woman's face, and a broom sweeping darkness from a house. Al-Raghib, reported by Bursevi, distinguishes safara for removing a physical covering from asfara for a color becoming clear and bright; Bursevi says isfar can mean entering dawn time. Al-Samin calls the removal of darkness from dawn's face a metaphor. Ibn al-Sumayfi and Isa ibn al-Fadl's safara is explained by Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi as stripping darkness from dawn's face. Qut al-qulub, reported by Bursevi, describes the second dawn as the sun's white glow beneath red twilight before the solar disk appears: sunset goes red, white, dark, and sunrise reverses the sequence. Al-Tabatabai calls isfar dawn's clearing and unveiling. Al-Damghani glosses asfara as dawn brightening and becoming clear. Al-Suyuti's Itqan reports a proposed etymology of tafsir from reversed safar, illustrated by dawn brightening; he also reports derivations from fasr and a physician's diagnostic test.

# 12:36/q21 What does 'wine' mean as the thing pressed, and how is the wording explained? [أَعْصِرُ خَمْرًۭا · meaning]
turns on: Whether khamr directly names grapes, anticipates wine, abbreviates a construction, or names the intended product.
- 12:36/q21/p1 It means grapes in a dialect, especially Oman or Azd Oman.
  reasons: Al-Asmaʿi's Bedouin called carried grapes khamr; al-Dahhak says the Quran uses several peoples' speech. Some name Ghassan and Azd Oman, while Ibn al-Qasim says Quraysh knew it. This explains the object directly. Al-Zarkashī relays Ibn Durayd through al-Fārisī on the Azd Oman lexical usage and a view denying metaphor on that basis; al-Suyūṭī reports al-Ḍaḥḥāk's Omani gloss.

# 12:42/q01 Who expected one prisoner to survive, and how certain was that expectation? [ظَنَّ أَنَّهُۥ نَاجٍۢ مِّنْهُمَا · interpretation]
turns on: Whether ظن names Joseph's certainty or inference, or the prisoner's response to Joseph's revealed interpretation.
- 12:42/q01/p1 Joseph knew the cupbearer would survive; “thought” expresses certain knowledge or conviction.
  reasons: Al-Tabari says prophetic prediction cannot be falsely certain; Ibn Atiyya and al-Tabataba'i cite قضي الأمر; al-Tabrisi cites 69:20 and al-Alusi and al-Tabataba'i cite 2:46. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)) · author · prefers · Since other opening oaths name specific daytimes or night phases, ʿaṣr probably denotes a particular time rather than time in general. «stellt wohl auch ʿaṣr eine spezifische Zeitangabe dar und bezeichnet nicht allgemein „Zeitspanne“»
[CORPUSCORANICUM:103:1:anmerkung/r4] CORPUSCORANICUM (Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)) · author · holds · If ʿaṣr means late afternoon, this oath differs from all other early Meccan oaths naming night or stages of morning and forenoon. «Falls wirklich der Spätnachmittag intendiert ist, so hebt sich Q 103 von allen anderen frühmekkanischen Schwüren»
[RAZI-FULL:v32p81/r1] RAZI-FULL (Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī, d. 606) · أبو مسلم · reports · Abu Muslim reads العصر as one end of the day, the afternoon, paired with the morning's signs of resurrection, judgment, and the evening's signs of death and destruction. «وهو قول أبي مسلم : المراد بالعصر أحد طرفي النهار»

[BIQAI-FULL:v8p521#s103/r2] BIQAI-FULL (al-Biqāʿī, d. 885) · author · holds · The surah distinguishes the saved human essence from the doomed and teaches salvation by leaving the transient for the lasting; the name al-ʿAṣr signals extraction of an essence. «مقصودها تفضيل نوع الإنسان المخلوق من علق ، وبيان خلاصته وعصارته»
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p522/r1] BIQAI-FULL (al-Biqāʿī, d. 885) · author · holds · The surah continues al-Takāthur's warning about worldly pleasures and the threat of Hell: people in this life face grave danger and their pleasures are clouded. «ختم التكاثر عن ذلك النعيم متوعدا برؤية الجحيم»
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p522/r2] BIQAI-FULL (al-Biqāʿī, d. 885) · author · reports · Al-ʿAṣr may mean the time when Adam was created, on Friday afternoon according to a sound report in Muslim; the middle prayer or its time; the Prophet's era; each person's lifetime; the late afternoon; or all time. «أي الزمان الذي خلق فيه أصله آدم عليه الصلاة والسلام وهو في عصر يوم الجمعة كما ورد في الحديث الصحيح في مسلم»
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p522/r3] BIQAI-FULL (al-Biqāʿī, d. 885) · author · holds · The afternoon is valuable because work ends, rest begins, daily gains are gathered, and the day's remaining hours reveal who used their time profitably; the word can also evoke resurrection. «أو وقت الأصيل لأنه أفضله بما يحويه من الفراغ من الأشغال واستقبال الراحة»
[BINTSHATI:v2p75/r2] BINTSHATI (ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ), d. 1419) · author · holds · The root sense of asr is pressing to extract juice, as in squeezing grapes; related words name the press, place of pressing, and stones used for it. «والمعنى الأصلي للعصر لغة: الضغط لاستخلاص العصارة»
[BINTSHATI:v2p75/r6] BINTSHATI (ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ), d. 1419) · author · holds · Quranic uses of the root include squeezing grapes in Yusuf 12:36 and rain clouds in al-Naba 78:14, alongside the verb in Yusuf 12:49. «بمعناه اللغوي الأول في اعتصار الخمر بآية يوسف 36»
[BINTSHATI:v2p76/r1] BINTSHATI (ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ), d. 1419) · author · holds · The root also appears for a whirlwind in al-Baqara 2:266 and for asr in the surah itself. «والإعصار في آية البقرة 266. والعصر، في سورة العصر»
[JISHUMI:v10p7529/r4] JISHUMI (al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī, d. 494) · author · holds · Al-ʿaṣr means time, from wringing moisture out of cloth; the image is extended to time as the span in which affairs are worked and turned. «العصر: الدهر، وأصله: عصر الثوب ونحوه، وهو فتله لإخراج مائه»
[ELMALILI:103:1-3/r4] ELMALILI (Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır, d. 1361) · author · holds · Vocalization variants asr, isr, and usr can mark a specific time; paired asran can refer to day and night or morning and evening. «Gündüzle geceye ve sabah ile akşama “asrân” denilir.»
[ELMALILI:103:1-3/r5] ELMALILI (Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır, d. 1361) · author · holds · With the generic article, al-asr may include every sense; with the covenant article, it may identify one particular time. «Lâm-ı cins ile وَٱلْعَصْرِ makāmına göre bunların her birinin cinsine»
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p528/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL (Ibn ʿĀshūr, d. 1393) · author · holds · “Time” has several possible referents; whichever is intended, its significance comes from being a period that manifests divine action, by contextual indication, addition, or shared reference. «وللعصر معانن يتعين أن يكون المراد منها»
[ASAD-NOTES:103:1/r1] ASAD-NOTES (Muhammad Asad, d. 1412) · author · holds · Unlike dahr, which denotes unlimited time without beginning or end, asr signifies passing time that cannot be recovered. «dahr, which signifies "unlimited time", without beginning or end: i.e., "time absolute"). Hence, asr bears the connotation of the passing or the flight of time - time which can never be recaptured»

[ELMALILI:103:1-3/r3] ELMALILI (Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır, d. 1361) · author · holds · As a noun, asr can mean the whole age, day and night, parts of the day, afternoon prayer or time, a group, and rain; as a verb it can mean restraining, preventing, taxing, or squeezing out juice. «Kāmûs’ta zikrolunduğu üzere “asr” kelimesi lügatta isim olarak dehr»
[ELMALILI:103:1-3/r6] ELMALILI (Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır, d. 1361) · author · holds · In Turkish usage asr commonly means time generally, the present era, or a period of eighty or a hundred years. «Ondan dolayı lisânımızda “asr” mutlak zaman ve bilhassa içinde bulunulan zaman»
[BINTSHATI:v2p75/r3] BINTSHATI (ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ), d. 1419) · author · holds · Arabic also calls rain-bearing clouds mu'sirat, says a people asaru when they bring rain, and uses i'sar for a strong wind driving clouds. «وسميت السحب الممطرة معصرات لما تعتصر من المطر، وأعصر القوم أمطروا»
[BINTSHATI:v2p75/r5] BINTSHATI (ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ), d. 1419) · author · holds · The age is called asr because experience and hardship press out a person's essence; late afternoon is also asr as the day is brought to its close, and the prayer takes its name from that time. «سمي الدهر عصراً، بملحظ من استخلاصه عصارة الإنسان بالضغط والتجربة»
